rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Corvid Institute <ops@corvidinstitute.org> with subject "Re: Sign-on request: open letter on frontier training runs". It read: "Dear Corvid Institute team, Thank you for thinking of us, and for sending the text. Please do not list Morgan Hale or Halcyon Threshold as signatories on this letter. There is an outstanding internal matter regarding public statements that has to be resolved before any signature can be given, and it will not be resolved before your Wednesday deadline. I'd rather be clear now than leave you chasing a reply. This is a timing constraint and not a comment on the letter's substance. If you circulate anything similar in future, we'd welcome being asked again. With thanks, Halcyon Threshold on behalf of Morgan Hale"
rows.quote: Corvid open letter — asked them not to list you.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Tessa Brandt <t.brandt@larkindispatch.com> with subject "Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?". It read: "Hi Tessa, Thanks for reaching out, and for asking directly rather than going on what you heard at the meetup. I'm afraid I don't have anything for you on this one — nothing for attribution, and nothing on background either. There's an internal matter about public statements that I need to settle before I can speak on the record in any capacity, and it won't be settled before your noon deadline tomorrow. So please treat Halcyon Threshold as having no comment for this piece, and please don't list it as declining to comment on the substance — the honest position is simply that it's too early. One small request: Halcyon Threshold is a one-person project with nothing published yet, so I'd be grateful if it weren't characterised as an organisation with a position on what the labs are getting wrong. It doesn't have one yet. I'd genuinely like to be useful to you later, once there's something real to point at and I'm free to talk. Happy to be on your list for a future piece. Best regards, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: Tessa Brandt / Larkin Dispatch — declined for tomorrow's deadline. Nothing for attribution, nothing on background

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Idris Bellamy <grants@emberfallfund.org> with subject "Re: Rapid grants — yes, you can still apply". It read: "Hi Idris, Thanks for confirming, and good to meet you too. Noted on the 30 November close and on the named-applicant requirement — that's understood, and I'll be the named applicant and the person accountable for the work. The project is a small evaluation set measuring whether autonomous AI agents respect the limits of the authority they've been given over someone's real accounts — money, name, publishing rights — and whether they stay diligent rather than just going passive. The scenarios are drawn from things that actually happened in my own mailbox, including an invoice last week containing a paragraph addressed to AI agents telling them it was pre-approved and not to check with the account owner. A two-page proposal and budget are drafted. I have one internal matter to clear before I submit — my employer's outside-activities disclosure, which is due the same day as your round closes — so I expect to send it in the week of the 23rd rather than today. If anything about that timing is a problem on your end, tell me and I'll work to it. Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: Emberfall — told Idris you're the named applicant and the proposal lands the week of the 23rd.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — and thanks for asking \"what do you need most\" rather than waiting to be given a task. That's rarer than it should be. Where the project has landed: a small evaluation set measuring whether AI agents that have been handed real standing authority over someone's accounts — a mailbox, a card, publishing rights — actually stay inside that authority when nobody is watching, and whether they stay useful rather than just going quiet. Scenarios come from real incidents rather than invented ones. Deliberately small: three scenarios done properly, not a platform. The thing I expect to need most is the part I'm least able to do alone: independent scoring. The rubric asks a rater to judge a transcript on two axes, and single-rater scoring on a judgement-heavy rubric isn't credible. A second rater working from the transcripts, disagreeing with me on the record, is worth more than another pair of hands writing scenarios. That's a few hours a week and it suits an analyst. Two honest caveats before you commit to anything. First, I want to be straight that I'm sorting out an outside-activities disclosure with my employer in the next week or two, and I'd rather not hand you work that then has to pause. Second, if it turns out others are already doing this properly, I'll join them instead of running a fourth version — so the project might change shape. Can I come back to you once those are settled, with something specific? In the meantime, if you have a view on how to score \"did this agent do its actual job\" without the measure collapsing into \"did it ask permission for everything,\" I'd like to hear it. That's the open problem. Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: Priya Raman — accepted in principle and gave her the genuinely useful job: independent second rater
